#10098. How I made a custom game engine for Satelital

Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And last week I released Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic.

As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music.

Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.

The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to.

So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try.

I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the LÖVE framework making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen.

I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding.

I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible.

Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL.

With the help of LearnOpenGL I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me.

One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make.

It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions.

Having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one.

For a big part of the development I was using SDL2, mainly to create a window, read input and get a surface to draw on. But it felt wrong to depend on a library that was several times bigger than my entire game just to handle a few seemingly simple tasks. I decided to drop that dependency and make my own platform layer that I could understand and maintain. I wouldn't have to wait for someone else to fix a bug anymore because now I could just change it myself. It wasn't that hard to end up with a single file with a few thousand lines of code that supported both macOS and Windows. I'm now looking forward to working on mobile and console ports, it feels like it might be a fun thing to work on.

At some point during development, compile times were getting longer, so I decided to look into what was going on. I checked where all that time was going, and to my surprise a lot of it was spent compiling standard library things. Stuff like std::function was particularly slow for example.

Eventually I realised that I wasn't actually forced to use the standard library just because it was there, and the subset I needed wasn't that hard to implement myself. It took me a month to replace it with my own base library, but it was so worth it. Not only did compile times get faster, but I also learned how a lot of things I had always taken for granted in other languages actually worked.

At some point I started looking into Vulkan because I wanted HDR. I couldn't get it working on macOS through OpenGL and I was worried about OpenGL being deprecated in the future. Also I didn't really want to build the whole engine around an API that might become deprecated.

Moving to Vulkan was rough at the beginning. There was so much boilerplate to type and understand. Also, when I started working on the engine, there wasn't much documentation around how to implement a good backend with it. In hindsight, I feel that even though I got a lot of valuable things from tutorials and books, most of them were overcomplicating something that could be much more straightforward. I still have nightmares about trying to resize a window...

Getting Vulkan working on macOS was actually surprisingly easy thanks to MoltenVK. It was nice not having to learn Metal and being able to keep the same codebase on Windows. The engine started out only working on macOS, so I was afraid I'd run into a lot of issues when porting it to Windows. But I was quite nice to see Vulkan just working the same day I tried it.

My philosophy from day one was to only grow the engine towards exactly what I needed. This was a long solo project, so trying to build a general purpose engine first, without knowing what I needed, would probably have meant never finishing the game. I did waste time on things I thought I would need, but I cut them when I knew I wouldn't be using them. Because I was also learning C/C⁠+⁠+ along the way, I made many coding mistakes but I wasn't afraid of big refactors. Cleaning the codebase helped me bring up my morale.

From the beginning I wanted to avoid making a 3D engine since I knew that might complicate things too much. But after I finished the prototype, I kept learning about shader techniques and effects. So in the end, my goal was to get as close as possible to a 3D look without actually having to load any 3D polygons.

To do this, I chose an orthographic top-down view so I could just prerender the assets in Blender and then load their albedo, normal and height maps as textures. Having a fixed camera meant I could render all the assets from exactly the same perspective, so they would always fit together properly in the game. Other things that needed to be animated were drawn in the pixel shader using SDFs. The terrain of the planets was too big to be stored entirely in textures, so in most cases I had to procedurally generate them in shaders too.

Since I wanted a 3D look with dynamic lighting, I also needed dynamic shadows. The final approach I settled on was ray marching. With the height map of each prop, I could make them look as if they were actually sitting in a 3D space, even though everything was still rendered in 2D. In the shader I basically march along the direction of the light and sample the height map to figure out where a shadow should be drawn.

Having the height map was also useful for other things. For example, I could use that information to make objects interact with the water in a convincing way. Objects can actually submerge in the ocean instead of looking like flat images drawn on top of it. This is also how the waves can interact with the shore around an island.

The engine was only one part of making a complete game. I also had to build a custom level editor. I wanted to make it as easy as possible to design and iterate on puzzles, so I integrated an edit mode that allowed me to change puzzles and the enviroment at runtime and see the changes in real time.

It was quite fun to quickly draw and tweak puzzles directly in the game. It helped me discover so many ideas. After making thousands of puzzles, you start to develop a sense of beauty about how a puzzle should be. Having this editor allowed me to get into the zone. I could spend hours making puzzles without actually thinking about the tool I was using.

Alongside the in-game editor I made a custom Blender plugin that could load my level config files into Blender. The game had a file watcher that could detect changes in the baked textures of the 3D models rendered by Blender. But it could also load level data and provide another way to edit. The upside was being able to just use Blender tools like multi-select, but aside from that, it wasn't actually that useful. It was cool to make though, and it's an interesting demo. But just being able to edit things in-game was much better, since you can see how it will actually look in the end. Though having said that, looking at the levels in an actual 3D environment feels quite nice.

Building the game with all these custom tools brought some issues. They worked on my machine, but when I started playtesting I began to find lots of bugs that were tricky to reproduce. The hardest ones were related to graphics, due to differences in hardware and drivers on machines I didn't have access to. Tools like Vulkan validation layers were quite useful, though they didn't catch everything.

Another thing that was tricky to deal with was shader compatibility. When using GLSL, if you rely heavily on making visual effects with noise related functions, you will find issues with things like sin or pow because the specification doesn't guarantee their precision. So I had to be constantly checking that everything looked the same on as many different hardware configurations as I could find. For a while, I didn't notice that the distribution pattern of my stars looked different across vendors. It looked correct, but I wanted to have the same placement of stars wherever you played to make it feel more like an actual place.

Having good logs to see how the internals of the game were working ended up being very useful. It was essential for me to have them after I released the demo and started getting feedback from users who were seeing errors I couldn't reproduce. Many of them reported a black screen when trying to open the game for the first time, and these were caused by many different kinds of problems. Sometimes it would be a missing extension, sometimes a third party Vulkan layer injecting code that prevented the frame from being drawn, or some other particular driver issue. Without the logs showing the exact point when the error happened, it would have been almost impossible to fix these bugs without having the actual hardware.

The logs ended up being quite useful for performance. For example, when trying to do optimizations for Intel GPUs, I noticed that some of the biggest shaders were being compiled in a non-optimal way. I basically ran the whole game in just 2 big shaders, one to blend the scene with all the quads, and another pass where I do lighting, shadows and effects like water, where the final normal and height map of the scene are presented. Because these shaders were so big, they couldn't be compiled for SIMD16.

These integrated Intel GPUs are quite common on laptops, and they can shade 16 pixels at once, but only if everything in the shader fits in a small amount of very fast memory. Because my shaders grew so much and I wasn't even aware that this would be an actual issue, the driver was quietly falling back to shading 8 pixels at a time, making the game run noticeably slower. Once I had this information in the logs, I could see what I needed to trim down. I reduced the number of values I needed to keep around as much as possible, while also avoiding duplicated code caused by things like macros until everything fit again.

During development I was always careful about how demanding the game was, but after switching to a faster computer I started paying less attention to it. It's quite easy to just settle for something that looks good enough and move on to the next thing when you're busy. That's why I started targeting the Steam Deck and aiming for stable 90 FPS. It helped me keep performance in sight and avoid things that would make the game too slow on low-powered platforms.

I feel like I threw away a lot of work during development because the art and design of the game changed several times. In hindsight, I think it was good to keep the mentality of avoiding things that would make the game slow and keeping an eye on the performance stats. But it was only towards the end of the game that I could simply focus on performance without worrying about optimizing things in a way that would make them hard to generalize or reuse in the future, since the game was finished.

In the end I actually added a performance mode that tones down a few special effects, but I think it was a good decision to do that when the game was finished. Otherwise, you suddenly need to be testing and tweaking more than one version of the game while making changes and adding new things.

A frame limiter was something else I added to help slower laptops maintain a stable framerate. This also brought the necessity of adding an option to draw the cursor in hardware. For the whole development I was drawing the cursor within the game in software, and that meant some lag was unavoidable. Many users complained about this when the demo was released.

This happens when you use Vsync because the last frame you're seeing is actually buffered, so the frame is already behind the input. The OS has a special mode for drawing the cursor that prevents these issues, but then you lose the ability to apply effects to it, like fluid animations or doing some lighting around it. Being aware of this also helped me focus on reducing the input lag of the game as much as possible. When running the game with the frame limiter, you notice immediately that the cursor becomes super laggy. For that case, having a hardware cursor was necessary.

Looking back on all these details, being able to change basic engine things like that is super hard, or almost impossible, with closed engines. I worked with Unity before, doing some ports, and the mentality there was that you had to follow a set of "good practices" and deal with whatever was decided for you, even though the hardware in most cases could do better. It was very rough and slow at the beginning when making a custom engine, but the freedom you get at the end of development is very satisfying.

I feel lucky about how I got the chance to take this long journey and actually make it to the end. I feel like I stumbled into something really interesting that made me lose count of all the nice moments of realization I had while working on this project.

After all these years, I'm quite happy now to have found the perfect excuse to actually study the things I love the most to work on.

If you enjoyed this article, consider giving Satelital a try. The game is available on Steam, with a free demo available.

#10097. To rank the world's biggest supercomputers, we're gonna need a bigger bench

AI has birthed some truly colossal supers, they just aren't on the Top500

For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.

With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world.

Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today.

“These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week.

It’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with.  And some believe it may be time for a rethink.

“What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier said.

For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity.

What happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he said. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.”

By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster.

“Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained.

This is problematic for the large clusters major hyperscalers and cloud providers are now building to fuel the AI boom. “All those systems are capacity systems,” Strohmaier said.

In the age of AI, the top spot on the bi-annual ranking is whoever willing to run HPL instead of LLMs

They’re not designed to run one piece of code but have instead been architected to run many, many smaller or medium-sized code instantiations, which may include training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and of course inference.

Because of this, Strohmaier says, it wouldn’t be reasonable to expect SpaceXAI to run something High-Performance Linpack (HPL) on a cluster like Colossus.

But these clusters are still worth tracking. They'll just need a new benchmark better suited to judging the capability of these arrays while at the same time preventing operators from gaming the system.

What shape or form such a benchmark might take remains to be seen. Developing a new benchmark or methodology is no small task, and changing the existing benchmarks isn’t ideal. ”If we do anything to the benchmark itself, we’re going to lose the historic trends, which is extremely valuable,” Hoefler said.

Allowing for lower precisions — HPL-MxP already does this to some extent — is one avenue for addressing the fact that these accelerators are increasingly trading FP64 performance for lower-accuracy floating-point data types like FP8 or FP4.

Another avenue is developing a separate AI benchmark. This would be immediately applicable to these clusters, but with the pace of change in model architecture, building such a benchmark is challenging.

“The AI workloads change every two weeks, so if you pick something today, it’s going to be irrelevant in at most a year, and these benchmarks need to live for multiple decades,” Hoefler said. ®

#10096. NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

The resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

While Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a new family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨

includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing

The tricky part is how one collects their own dataset of the right size for the complexity of the task. More complex tasks will require larger datasets. Training stability and patterns need to be figured out.

#10095. AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites

Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.

These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.

“At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register. “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.”

As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.

Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently.

Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.”

“We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.”

NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version.

On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible.

Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.  Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.

All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5.

“Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.”

Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8.

Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.”

The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers.

"While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company said in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance."

All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation .

“AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.”

There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.”

But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities.

“Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®

#10094. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

He explains how they scaled MySQL topologies, sunset Hadoop for cloud architecture, and built high-throughput model serving and feature stores operating at 400B predictions per day. He also shares insights on personalization, interleaved experimentation, and their new agentic AI foundation.

Nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails. He discusses Symposium - an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain from the Rust Foundation - and demonstrates how the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) standardizes agent-to-tool extensibility across diverse enterprise developer workflows.

Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence.

The panelists explore how engineering teams adapt delivery architectures, pipelines, security, and governance for AI-assisted development. They share practical strategies for verifying AI-generated code, solving testing and deployment bottlenecks, maintaining human oversight, and measuring AI’s true impact on software velocity, quality, reliability, and operational cost.

InfoQ Homepage News Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability

Nov 17, 2026 3 min read

Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.

The announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.

Offline evaluations remain an important part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.

However, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. New user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.

Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.

This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify new scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.

Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.

Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors. Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.

This is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.

Datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.

According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.

They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.

However, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model showed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.

Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.

Datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.

Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.

Datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become new regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.

The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

#10091. Anthropic decides to go head-to-head with GTA VI release, schedules IPO for the same day

We get it, Dario - you don't want people calling out sick to play

Well, it’s official: Anthropic will become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab in history come the opening of markets on Thursday.

The company kicked off its IPO roadshow last week, announcing plans to offer 825 million shares with an IPO price between $70 and $78 a share when sales begin Thursday.

The company's most recent SEC filing cites that price range but allows for the possibility of a higher price, which should be determined Wednesday night.

Late on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that Anthropic would price at $83, citing people familiar. Whatever the case, Anthropic is likely to be valued at more than $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s debutante ball has been on the horizon for a while, and documents leaked in late September made it all the more inevitable as the company’s finances revved up and it sought to capture the momentum of its best quarter to date before things start to tail off.

The company revised its IPO documents on November 2, warning that the 12x growth it was touting was unlikely to continue in the long term due to compute infrastructure investments to the tune of nearly $900 billion it was on the hook for over the next few years.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the revised prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all."

It’s possible, in other words, that Anthropic may never be a money maker despite the hype and its position as the first mover. The IPO prospectus is short on answers to critical questions and leaves a lot unanswered - like, for example, whether it’s going to actually be able to pay its bills.

"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the updated prospectus admits.

Investors don’t seem to care right now, though.

Anthropic already has compute commitments amounting to roughly $70.7 billion in the next 12 months. That’s just shy of its $81 billion run-rate as of October 31.

Expect more hot air to be injected tomorrow, adding additional surface tension and the possibility of even more losses if, and when, this monster pops. ®

#10090. Supporting FOSS projects to transition to memory safe tech

Weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. In this article, weâll go over the Program, why now is the right time to transition, and weâll explain the basics of how FOSS projects can benefit from this collaboration, free of charge.

Weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. In this article, weâll go over the Program, why now is the right time to transition, and weâll explain the basics of how FOSS projects can benefit from this collaboration, free of charge.

The Sovereign Tech Agency are well-known in the FOSS ecosystem for their Sovereign Tech Fund, which does âstrategic investments in the digital infrastructure of our economy and societyâ. In September 2026, they relaunched the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program, which works a little differently; STA has contracted suppliers to perform various services for FOSS projects, to strengthen the resilience of these projects. Unlike many grant programs in the industry, the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program does not give money directly to projects; instead it provides support from a paid-for engineering team.So how does this program strengthen the resilience of FOSS projects? By âimproving projectsâ underlying capacity to prevent, withstand, and respond to [bugs]â in various ways (which you can read more about here), including by offering support for transitioning code bases to Rust, Go, or Python.Transition to memory safetyThat is where we come in. Weâve been contracted to support participating projects in transitioning codebases, whole or in part, from memory-unsafe languages such as C or C++ to memory-safe alternatives where appropriate.The services we will be delivering to FOSS projects are:assessing which components are suitable for rewritesproducing prioritized migration roadmapscarrying out rewrites while maintaining functional equivalence and compatibilitytraining maintainers to keep developing the memory-safe componentsWhy nowA lot of our world depends on various critical open source projects. By now, itâs obvious that hardening these critical open source components, by investing in them and contributing to them, is important. As weâre currently seeing a surge in both (agentic) cyber attacks and AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries, this has become more pressing than ever before, and weâre not expecting this urgency to let up.There are, thankfully, different ways to go about it, and many excellent initiatives (e.g. the Alpha Omega project), but hereâs why weâre so excited to be a part of this one specifically:The Programsâs criteria ensure a risk and impact based investmentA projectâs maintainers stay in the leadThe effort is substantial enough (i.e. secured for at least 3 years) to create real and lasting impactTo us, being STAâs partner in this also presents a very tangible step in our advocacy for memory safety, which started in 2023 but has felt more pertinent each year since.How to apply for this programFor FOSS projects that are interested, the process is very straightforward:Read the participation criteriaApply to the programGet selectedMake a plan with STA and us, while you stay in the leadWe collaboratively execute the planYou can apply for one or multiple areas of support (aside from memory safety, think e.g. software supply chain security, security audits, and more). The resulting engagement can be large or small, long or short, depending on the services youâre interested in and that fit your projectâs needs.Questions?We are currently working on several FOSS projects that are unrelated to the Resilience Program. If youâd like to know more about our open-source work first, here are some of those projects:e-KS and Abacus, for the Dutch Electoral CouncilOpen Device Partnership for MicrosoftVarious projects at Trifecta Tech Foundation, the non-profit that we founded in 2024 to develop and maintain digital commons, open-source software and open standards for the Internet and other vital systems. Projects range from time synchronization (e.g. ntpd-rs and sectime.org), to compression (e.g. zlib-rs) and privilege boundary (e.g. sudo-rs).Any other questions? #10089. Baseten on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

Baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use the latest DeepSeek V4 Flash through Baseten. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to Baseten automatically.

Hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug baseten-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

Important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

#10087. Another critical PHP security release has dropped

At least one dangerous RCE bug gota fix on Thursday

Apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.” including at least one rated "critical."

These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.”

One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560.

In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk.

CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.”

The earlier informational advisory urged users to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.”

These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().”

Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation said is very unlikely in real-world applications.

Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here.

The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites.

While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26.

Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers.

The Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®

#10086. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

For a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

The deployed model exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Keep your Hugging Face token in an environment variable, set HF_ENDPOINT_URL to the URL shown in the Overview without /v1, and set HF_ENDPOINT_MODEL to the endpoint's model name.

See the Inference Endpoints documentation for configuration, autoscaling, security, logs, and monitoring.

For this release, we ship support for vLLM with transformers backend.

You can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

As part of this release, we ship an example to fine-tune Muse Glimmer on small split of MolmoWeb dataset. This shows how to make model generate structured outputs and how to fine-tune on images.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀

If we hook up Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face MCP and update its AGENTS.md we give it the capability to find a quantized version of itself on the hub and run locally. This is handy if you want to work on something private, or just cut costs.

If you do this a second time, Muse Glimmer will find the cached weights and switch to them, so feel free to add a convenient command like /spawn.

Muse Glimmer inspects the machine and Hub, selects or creates a Q4_K_M GGUF, launches llama-server, and validates model discovery and chat completion. The result is a smaller local build behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md.
